source.title_on_document: Generative AI as an External Cognitive Tool for Developing Creative Intelligence in Visual Design: A Mixed-Methods Randomized Study Using Cognitive Load Indicators and Motivational Modeling

supplement.where: The paper mentions no supplementary material. Data Availability Statement (p. 28): "Data are contained within the article."

paper_design_summary: 120 second-year visual communication design undergraduates were randomly assigned as individuals to two separately taught classes of 60 for a six-week illustration course: a GenAI-embedded design-thinking course (GenAI built into all five design-thinking stages, workshops, group work) or a traditional course in which GenAI was used only sporadically. Six experts rated the 24 final group projects (12 per arm) on five dimensions (creativity, applicability, technicality, expressiveness, completeness) on a 100-point scale. Students also answered end-of-course cognitive-load and ARCS motivation questionnaires analyzed with PLS-SEM.

studies.label: Six-week illustration course experiment (GenAI-integrated vs traditional instruction)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Instructional model for a six-week Illustration Design course: GenAI-embedded design-thinking course (experimental) vs traditional illustration teaching with only sporadic GenAI use (control). Each arm was taught as a separate class by the same lecturers.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned at the individual level into an experimental group and a control group, with 60 students in each group, and the two groups were taught in separate classes.

arms.name: Experimental (Integrated Teaching Model)
arms.description: GenAI-embedded instructional model built on the five design-thinking stages (Empathize-Define-Ideate-Prototype-Test) with explicit tool-intervention points ('task chain + tool chain'); workshop-based teaching, group collaboration, iterative cycles, process-oriented evaluation (Table 2, p. 11).

arms.name: Control (Traditional Teaching Model)
arms.description: Traditional illustration-teaching process; lecturer-led instruction and case analysis; GenAI tools used only sporadically (e.g., sketch generation, style reference) while manual drawing and conventional digital software dominate (p. 10, Section 3.4.3; Table 2, p. 11).

participants.exclusions: None reported. Tables 1 and 7 report n = 60 per group, and the SEM analysis uses n = 120 students. The creativity outcome is analyzed at the project level: 24 final group projects (12 per arm, Table 13). The paper does not state how many students are in each project team or whether all 120 students are covered by the 24 projects.
participants.who: Second-year undergraduates majoring in Visual Communication Design, same major and cohort, enrolled in the Illustration Design course in one semester at 'College X', volunteers
participants.country: not_stated (authors and the approving IRB are at Hanyang University, Republic of Korea)
participants.quote: This study recruited 120 s-year undergraduate students majoring in Visual Communication Design at College X as the research participants.
participants.locator: p. 9, Section 3.4 and 3.4.1; Table 1, p. 10 (n = 60 per group)

ai_tool.name_model: not_stated for the intervention (baseline survey names Midjourney, DALL-E, ChatGPT-4 as examples of mainstream GenAI tools, p. 9)
ai_tool.how_used: GenAI embedded across all course stages to support information gathering, idea generation, visual production, and feedback analysis (p. 7); experts and the paper attribute differences to rapid generation and iteration of visual solutions (pp. 12, 21). Control group used GenAI only sporadically for sketch generation or style reference.

task.description: Final group illustration-design project in the Illustration Design course; works presented to experts as final images, brief design statements, and key process summaries.
task.duration: Six-week course; same teaching weeks, in-class hours, assignment windows, and deadline for both groups (p. 12)

outcomes.name: Overall expert evaluation score of final project (mean of five dimensions)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Six experts with teaching and industry experience in illustration and visual communication rated anonymized works in randomized order in one on-site panel session on a 100-point scale; the project score is the mean of five dimensions (creativity, applicability, technicality, expressiveness, completeness). The abstract calls this 'expert-rated creative performance', but the composite mixes creativity with craft and quality dimensions. ICC(2,k) = 0.924, 95% CI [0.847, 0.947]; ICC(2,1) = 0.670 (Table 14, p. 22). p. 20 also says discrepancies were resolved through discussion until consensus.

contrasts.reported: Experimental M = 86.58, SD = 1.84 vs control M = 79.94, SD = 2.98; independent-sample t-test at project level (n = 24), t(22) = 6.57, p < 0.001; Cohen's d = 2.68. Per-project scores in Table 13 (12 Exp, 12 Ctrl).
contrasts.locator: p. 20, Section 4.6; Table 13, p. 21; Figure 6 ('Final grade' panel), p. 22

outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Rubric dimension labeled 'Creativity', evaluation focus 'Novelty of concept and visual expression': 'Evaluates the uniqueness and degree of innovation in conceptual thinking, narrative logic, and visual language' (Table 3, p. 12). Same six experts and 100-point scale as S1-O1.

contrasts.reported: No arm means, SDs, or test printed. Table 13 lists each project's mean Creativity score: Exp W01-W12 range 82.17 to 89.83; Ctrl W13-W24 range 73.50 to 85.33. Text: experimental group has higher median scores than control across all dimensions; in Creativity the experimental group shows narrower IQRs.

eligibility.reason: Students were randomized individually (computer randomization of student IDs, p. 9) to a GenAI-embedded course vs a traditional course with only sporadic GenAI use; 120 people randomized and 120 analyzed in the questionnaire analyses (60 per arm). Experts rated the final works on creativity and other dimensions (pp. 11-12, 20-22). Caveats: the rated outcome covers only 24 group projects (12 per arm), so the effective sample for the creativity outcome is 24 teams; each arm was taught as one separate class, so arm and class coincide; the treatment bundles GenAI with a different pedagogy (design-thinking workshops, group collaboration, process assessment); the control arm also had sporadic GenAI access.

one_line_finding: Final group projects from the GenAI-integrated course received higher expert scores than those from the traditional course (mean of five dimensions 86.58, SD 1.84 vs 79.94, SD 2.98; t(22) = 6.57, p < 0.001, d = 2.68, n = 24 projects; p. 20), with higher medians on every dimension including Creativity (Table 13, p. 21; Figure 6, p. 22).
open_questions: Comparison type: coded ai_design because the control group also used GenAI 'sporadically' (p. 10; Table 2). The paper frames it as GenAI-integrated vs traditional instruction, so ai_vs_bau is arguable. The treatment also changes pedagogy (design thinking, workshops, group collaboration), so the contrast is not AI alone.

Construct of the 'Creativity' dimension: coded novelty because its rubric focus is 'Novelty of concept and visual expression' (Table 3, p. 12); overall_creativity is arguable given the label. The paper treats the five-dimension composite as 'expert-rated creative performance' (abstract); coded here as other.

Team composition and team size are not reported; the paper does not say whether every student contributed to one of the 24 projects. Table 2 describes the control task structure as 'Primarily based on independent assignments', yet 12 control group projects were rated.

Expert ratings are described as independent (pp. 12, 20), but p. 20 also says 'Discrepancies in scoring were resolved through iterative discussion until consensus was reached', which conflicts with computing an ICC on independent ratings.
Figure 6 caption text says scatter points are individual ratings by the six experts, but each panel appears to show about 12 points per group, which matches project-level means.
notes: Questionnaire outcomes (cognitive load IL/EL/GL, ARCS motivation AT/RE/CF/SA, ITA; Table 7, p. 15; PLS-SEM, MICOM, MGA in Tables 8-12) are self-reported and are not listed as outcomes. Baseline equivalence on prior GenAI use, prompt skill, a baseline design task, and motivation (Table 1, p. 10) shows no significant differences. The control group received the integrated course content after the experiment (p. 11). IRB: Hanyang University, approved 22 August 2025 (p. 28). Structured interviews with 2 lecturers and 10 experimental-group students (p. 13) are qualitative. No outcome was measured after AI was removed and no diversity-across-people outcome is reported.
